title: Which way is up?
hook: North sits at the top of almost every map today. Did mapmakers always put it there?

knows: that maps have north at the top
roughly where Europe, Asia and Africa are
doesNotKnow: that north-up is a convention that has changed
how medieval European world maps were laid out

misconception: North has always been up because that is the natural way to draw the world.
objective: The learner can explain that which direction is at the top of a map is a choice, and that medieval European world maps such as the Hereford map put east at the top.

claims.text: The Hereford world map (Hereford Mappa Mundi) dates from about 1300.
claims.source: Hereford Cathedral, 'The Mappa Mundi' (usually dated c. 1300). From memory, not checked online.

claims.text: The Hereford map puts Asia at the top, Europe at lower left and Africa at lower right.
claims.source: The map follows the T-O scheme: Asia fills the upper half, Europe the lower left quarter, Africa the lower right quarter (Hereford Cathedral; British Library 'T-O maps'). From memory, not checked online. Note: on the original, the labels for Europe and Africa are famously swapped; the layout of the land is as stated.

claims.text: The Hereford map, like other medieval European world maps, has east at the top.
claims.source: Hereford Cathedral; Harvey, Mappa Mundi: The Hereford World Map (1996). From memory, not checked online. The lesson also derives it: turning the globe so the layout in c2 holds puts east at the top (topDirection(90) in Demo.tsx).

claims.text: The Hereford map is centred on Jerusalem.
claims.source: Hereford Cathedral, 'The Mappa Mundi'. From memory, not checked online. Used for the stage caption and the globe's centre.

claims.text: The word 'orient' comes from the Latin for 'rising', the east, where the Sun rises.
claims.source: Oxford English Dictionary, 'orient': from Latin oriens, oriens -entis 'rising, sunrise, east', present participle of oriri 'to rise'. From memory, not checked online.

claims.text: Al-Idrisi drew his world map in 1154 with south at the top.
claims.source: The Tabula Rogeriana, made for Roger II of Sicily in 1154, is oriented with south at the top (Bodleian Library, MS. Pococke 375 copy). From memory, not checked online.

claims.text: North at the top is today's convention for almost every map.
claims.source: Hook and reveal. A statement about modern practice (national survey sheets, atlases, web maps all print north up by default). No source checked; needs one or softening.

claims.text: The Earth has no top, so which way is up on a map is a choice.
claims.source: A sphere has no preferred direction in space for a picture of it; the stage turns one orthographic view (d3-geo geoOrthographic, third rotation angle) and every turn is equally correct. The lesson makes no claim about why north-up won.

recall.question: Why is north at the top of most maps today?
options: The North Pole is the top of the Earth
It is a convention; medieval European maps put east at the top
Compasses only work with north up
recall.why: A ball has no top. Which way is up on a map is a choice, and it has changed: the Hereford map put east up, al-Idrisi put south up.
